pool.name: CS Fundamentals — Getting Started with a Computer
pool.description: 30 beginner questions: 10 easy, 10 medium, 10 hard. Each test draws two per difficulty. Covers physical devices, keyboard and mouse, desktop navigation, files, everyday applications, web basics, and a safe first project.

notes.title: 1. Understanding the Physical Computer
notes.summary: Identify the main parts, connect accessories safely, and start and shut down a computer.
notes.contentHtml:
Objective: use a computer confidently, one step at a time

You do not need previous computer experience. This topic teaches you to navigate a computer, manage simple files, and use a browser. Labels and button positions vary across Windows, macOS, Linux, and different devices; learn the purpose of each control rather than memorizing one screen.

Meet the parts

  • Monitor: the screen that shows text, pictures, and applications.
  • Keyboard: keys for entering text and commands.
  • Mouse or touchpad: moves the on-screen pointer and lets you select and move items.
  • System unit: the desktop case containing the processor, memory, and storage. It is not just the CPU: the CPU is one component inside.
  • Speakers or headphones: play sound. A microphone receives sound.
  • Webcam: captures video; many laptops have one above the screen.
  • Ports: sockets for power, accessories, displays, or audio.

Desktop versus laptop

A desktop commonly has a separate system unit, monitor, keyboard, and mouse. Some all-in-one desktops combine the computer and screen. A laptop combines its screen, keyboard, touchpad, and battery in one portable unit. Both can run applications and manage files. An external screen does not turn on the computer itself.

Recognize common connections

USB ports connect compatible devices such as keyboards and storage drives. USB-A is usually rectangular; USB-C is smaller and reversible. Some USB-C ports support charging or displays, but shape alone does not guarantee every feature. HDMI and DisplayPort commonly connect displays; a 3.5 mm audio socket may connect headphones or a headset. Consult the device labels or manual and never force a connector.

Start safely

  1. Place the computer on a stable surface and keep drinks away.
  2. Connect the manufacturer's recommended compatible power adapter if needed. Keep laptop ventilation openings clear.
  3. Press the computer's power button once and wait. A desktop monitor may have its own power button.
  4. Sign in using your own account. Keep passwords private; ask the owner or teacher for access to shared computers.

To finish, save your work and use the operating system's Shut down command. Closing a laptop lid or turning off a monitor may leave the computer running or asleep. Holding the power button can force power off and lose work; reserve it for recovery when normal shutdown is unavailable and seek help first.

Practice

Point to the screen, keyboard, pointer device, power button, and one port. Explain whether your device is a laptop, traditional desktop, or all-in-one. Do not open its case.

notes.title: 2. Using a Keyboard and Mouse
notes.summary: Practice selecting, opening, scrolling, dragging, typing, and familiar editing shortcuts.
notes.contentHtml:
Move and select with a mouse or touchpad

Move the mouse gently on a flat surface, or slide one finger on a touchpad, to move the pointer. Moving the pointer alone normally does not activate an item.

  • Click: press and release the primary button once to select an item or activate many controls.
  • Double-click: click twice quickly without moving much. Many desktop file managers open files this way; web links normally need only one click. Device settings can change this.
  • Right-click: use the secondary button to open a menu of actions for an item. A touchpad often uses a two-finger tap; settings vary.
  • Scroll: use the wheel or a supported touchpad gesture, often two fingers, to see content outside the visible area. Scroll direction can be configured.
  • Drag: point to an item, hold the primary button, move, and release. Practice moving a window by its title bar before dragging important files.

Find the keyboard keys

Letters and number keys enter text. Space adds a space; Enter starts a new paragraph in many editors or confirms an action in some dialogs. Backspace usually deletes before the insertion point; Delete behavior varies by keyboard. Arrow keys move the insertion point. Shift makes uppercase letters while held and selects the upper symbol on many keys; Caps Lock toggles letter case. Tab often moves keyboard focus between controls. Escape often dismisses a menu or cancels an action, but does not guarantee that changes are undone.

Ctrl, Alt, Command, and Option are modifier keys used with other keys. F1–F12 are function keys; some laptops require Fn to use particular functions. The exact layout and shortcuts depend on your keyboard, operating system, and application.

Common editing shortcuts

  • Copy: Ctrl+C on many Windows/Linux apps, Command+C on macOS.
  • Paste: Ctrl+V or Command+V.
  • Undo: Ctrl+Z or Command+Z.
  • Select all: Ctrl+A or Command+A.
  • Save: Ctrl+S or Command+S in many editors.

Hold the modifier, press the letter once, then release both. Copy puts a selection on the clipboard; it does not remove the original. Paste inserts it at the current destination. Select text before copying it, and place the insertion point where you want to paste. Save shortcuts do not save a web page form to your computer automatically.

Safe practice

In a blank text document, type I am learning to use a computer. Select the sentence by dragging across it, copy it, click after it, press Enter, and paste. Undo the paste. If a shortcut behaves differently, use the app's Edit or File menu to see its available commands.

notes.title: 3. Understanding the Desktop
notes.summary: Recognize windows and menus, switch between apps, and choose helpful accessibility settings.
notes.contentHtml:
Your workspace after sign-in

The desktop is the main workspace. An icon is a small picture representing an app, file, folder, or shortcut. A shortcut points to something; it is not necessarily a second copy of the original. Menus group available commands. A window is a visible area belonging to an application.

Find and open an application

Use your system's application launcher or search, such as Start on Windows or an application launcher on macOS/Linux. Type the application's name and select it. The taskbar or dock usually provides app launchers and indications of running apps, though its location and behavior can vary.

Manage windows

  • Minimize: hide a window from the main workspace without normally quitting its app. Restore it from the taskbar, dock, or window switcher.
  • Maximize: enlarge a window to use the available workspace. Full-screen mode is related but can behave differently; on macOS the green button often enters full screen.
  • Restore or resize: return to a smaller window or drag an edge where supported.
  • Switch: select another running app. Alt+Tab commonly switches windows on Windows/Linux; Command+Tab switches apps on macOS.
  • Close: close a window using its close control. Read save prompts carefully. Closing a window does not always quit the entire app, particularly on macOS.

Before typing, click the intended text field or window so it has focus. A shortcut acts on the focused app or control, not whichever app you are thinking about.

Settings and accessibility

Use Settings or System Settings to adjust volume, brightness, pointer size, text size, keyboard options, and network connections. Accessibility tools may include magnification, screen readers, high contrast, captions, on-screen keyboards, and alternatives to mouse input. They help many people work comfortably; they are not signs of failure.

Use Tab and Shift+Tab to move through many controls, then Enter or Space where appropriate. A visible focus indicator shows the selected control. Try built-in help to learn the accessibility tool for your system. Ask permission before changing a shared machine's settings and avoid changing security or administrator settings during practice.

Practice

Open a text editor and a calculator. Switch between them, minimize the editor, and restore it without opening a second document. Identify the difference between hiding a window, closing it, and shutting down the computer.

notes.title: 4. Files and Folders
notes.summary: Organize documents, understand names and paths, and distinguish local copies from cloud storage.
notes.contentHtml:
What are you saving?

A file is a named collection of data, such as a document, photograph, or song. A folder holds files and other folders to organize them. Use File Explorer on Windows, Finder on macOS, or your system's file manager to browse them.

Create and name

In a location you are allowed to use, choose New Folder or the equivalent menu command. Give it a meaningful name. Create a document in an app and use Save or Save As to choose its folder and filename. Avoid characters your system rejects, such as slashes used as path separators. A clear name like practice-notes.txt is easier to find than an unexplained name like new2.

Extensions and paths

  • .txt: plain text.
  • .pdf: a document format designed to preserve layout.
  • .jpg: a common image format.
  • .mp3: a common audio format.

An extension is a filename ending that helps applications recognize a format. It may be hidden in the file manager until you enable showing extensions. Renaming picture.jpg to picture.pdf does not convert the image into a PDF. A downloaded file's name or extension alone is not proof it is safe.

A path describes a location. For example, Documents/My First Computer Project/my-first-note.txt describes folders leading to a file; Windows commonly uses backslashes instead. Downloads is a folder often used by browsers, but the actual location can be changed. Check the save dialog or file manager rather than assuming every file is in Downloads.

Copy, move, rename, delete

  • Copy and paste: creates another copy at a destination; the original remains.
  • Move: changes the file's location. Use the file manager's supported Move command or an appropriate cut-and-paste workflow; platform behavior varies.
  • Rename: changes the name, not automatically the contents or format. Keep the intended extension.
  • Delete: often sends an item to Recycle Bin or Trash, where you may be able to restore it. Permanent deletion, some external drives, and some remote locations behave differently.

Dragging files can copy or move them depending on the locations and modifier keys. Use an explicit command and inspect the result while learning. Do not empty Trash or delete other people's files during practice.

Local versus cloud storage

Local storage is on your device or attached drive. Cloud storage uses a provider's remote systems, often with a local synced folder. A cloud file may be online-only or downloaded for offline access. Check its status. Synchronization is not the same as an independent backup: deleting a synced file can delete it across devices. Sharing a cloud file can grant others access; check permissions carefully.

Practice

Create a practice folder, save a small text file inside it, copy the file into another practice folder, and confirm the original still exists. Move only the practice copy back if desired. Say the folder path aloud to explain where your file lives.

notes.title: 5. Applications and Everyday Tasks
notes.summary: Write and save plain text, use a calculator, and understand trusted installation, updates, and permissions.
notes.contentHtml:
Applications help you do jobs

An application, or app, is software for a task such as writing, calculation, drawing, or browsing. The operating system manages the device and provides the environment where apps run.

Write and save a document

  1. Open a plain-text editor, such as Notepad on Windows, TextEdit in plain-text mode on macOS, or an available Linux text editor.
  2. Create a new document and type a few sentences.
  3. Choose Save or Save As. Select your intended folder, give the file a meaningful name ending in .txt, and confirm plain-text format if prompted.
  4. Make another edit and save again. The first save chooses a location; later saves commonly update that file.
  5. Close the document, reopen it from the file manager, and check that your latest text is present.

Some apps autosave; others do not. A title bar, saved indicator, or file information can help identify what is saved, but reopening the file is a useful practical check. Save As commonly creates a separately named version; after that, check which version you are editing. Read overwrite prompts before replacing an existing file.

Use the calculator

Open the system calculator. Enter 12 + 8 and select equals to obtain 20. Clear the calculation before starting another. Calculator modes and button layouts vary; a physical numeric keypad is optional.

Install and uninstall carefully

Prefer your operating system's trusted app store or the publisher's verified official site. Confirm the publisher and system requirements. Do not install from a random advertisement or follow an unexpected pop-up claiming your computer is infected. On shared, school, or work computers, ask the owner or administrator first; this lesson does not require installation.

Use the system's supported uninstall process or the app publisher's documented method. Deleting a shortcut usually removes only the shortcut, not the application. Uninstalling may leave user documents or settings; check the documented behavior before acting.

Updates and permissions

Updates may fix security problems, correct bugs, and improve features. Use trusted built-in update mechanisms, save work before a required restart, and allow time for updates to finish. A website banner is not automatically an authentic system update.

A permission grants access, such as microphone, camera, files, or location. Ask whether that access is necessary for the task. A video call may need microphone access; a simple calculator normally should not need your camera. Deny unexpected access and investigate. Do not bypass security warnings or enter administrator credentials just to complete this exercise.

Practice

Save a two-sentence .txt document and reopen it. Calculate 15 + 7. Explain why you would verify a publisher before installing and review camera access before allowing it.

notes.title: 6. Using the Web for the First Time
notes.summary: Distinguish browsers and search engines, navigate tabs and links, and safely handle downloads, uploads, and forms.
notes.contentHtml:
Four terms that make browsing easier

  • Browser: an application such as Firefox, Chrome, Edge, or Safari that opens web content.
  • Search engine: an online service used to find pages by keywords. A browser may use one from its address bar.
  • Website: a collection of related pages and resources, usually associated with a domain.
  • URL: a resource address, for example https://example.com. The address bar displays the location being visited.

A browser and a search engine are not the same thing. Typing keywords often performs a search; typing a full URL usually opens that location. Check the destination address, especially before signing in or uploading information. HTTPS encrypts the connection to the displayed site; it does not prove that the site or its claims are trustworthy.

Tabs, links, and navigation

A tab holds a page within a browser window. Use the plus button to open a new tab and the tab's close button to close it. Click a link once to navigate. Links may open a new tab or download a file instead. Back returns through that tab's browsing history; Reload requests the page again. Reloading can lose unsaved form entries or repeat a submission, so read confirmation prompts.

Downloads and uploads

Download: copy data from a remote system to your device. Use a trusted source, inspect the filename and format, and check the browser's download list or selected folder to find it. A download is not automatically safe to open. Avoid unknown installers and do not bypass browser warnings.

Upload: send a selected local file to a remote system. A Choose File button usually opens a file picker. Selecting a file may or may not immediately upload it; follow the site's instructions and check its confirmation. Upload only files you have permission to share and verify the exact filename and contents first.

Fill in a web form

  1. Check that you are on the intended site.
  2. Read field labels and required-field indicators.
  3. Click a field or use Tab to move between fields. Enter only necessary information.
  4. Review your entries and any attachment before choosing Submit.
  5. Look for confirmation or specific errors. Do not repeatedly submit if you are unsure whether the first submission succeeded.

Use a teacher-provided practice form with fictional information. Never submit real passwords, identity documents, bank details, or private files for this lesson. Saving a document locally is different from submitting it to a website.

Practice

Open https://example.com in a browser, identify the address bar, and open a second tab. On an approved practice site, describe which action would download a resource and which would upload your practice file. If no practice form is available, explain the steps without submitting anything.

notes.title: 7. Practical Project — My First Computer Project
notes.summary: Create, save, rename, and find a text document; complete a practical confidence checklist.
notes.contentHtml:
Your mission

Create a folder named My First Computer Project, save a text document inside it, rename the file, and find and reopen it. Use your own practice area. Do not delete, overwrite, or upload anyone's files. Set aside about 20 minutes; go slowly and repeat steps as needed.

Try these steps

  1. Open your file manager and choose an allowed location, such as your Documents folder. If your Documents folder is cloud-synced, note this and check the file's availability status.
  2. Create a new folder named My First Computer Project. If it already exists, inspect it and use a clearly named practice subfolder rather than overwriting existing work.
  3. Open a plain-text editor and create a new document. On TextEdit, choose plain-text mode. Type: My name is Learner. I can create and find a file. Use a fictional name if you prefer.
  4. Choose Save or Save As, navigate into your project folder, and save the document as my-first-note.txt in plain-text format. Avoid accidentally adding .txt twice if the editor supplies the extension.
  5. Add the sentence I saved my work. Save again, then close the document. If prompted about unsaved changes, review the prompt and save the intended version.
  6. In the file manager, locate the saved file and rename it to my-computer-practice.txt. Preserve the .txt extension; enable showing extensions if needed. If the destination name already exists, choose another unique name instead of replacing it.
  7. Navigate away from the project folder. Then find it again by following the folder path, or search for the exact filename. Check that the result is inside your project folder.
  8. Open the renamed file and confirm both the original text and the added sentence are present. Explain its location using the folder and filename.
  9. Open a browser, identify its address bar, and visit https://example.com. Open another tab, switch back, and close only the extra tab.

Optional safe extensions

Copy the text file to a second practice folder and confirm the original remains. If you want to practice deletion, delete only that extra practice copy after checking its name and location, then restore it from Recycle Bin or Trash where supported. Do not empty the bin. Explain an upload using a practice form without sending private data.

Troubleshooting

  • I cannot find my document: check the editor's recent-files list, the save location, and the exact filename. Search results may contain multiple copies; inspect the path.
  • My latest sentence is missing: check that you reopened the same version and saved after editing. An earlier saved copy will not contain unsaved changes.
  • The name ends in .txt.txt: show extensions, verify the file type, and correct the duplicate ending without changing the document format.
  • Something opens in an unexpected app: use Open With to choose a compatible text editor. Renaming the extension is not a reliable conversion method.
  • A cloud file will not open offline: reconnect and use the provider's supported download or keep-offline option before disconnecting.

Completion checklist

  • I can identify the main computer parts and shut down safely.
  • I can click, scroll, type, copy, paste, and save.
  • I can switch windows and restore a minimized app.
  • I can create a folder, save and rename a file, and find its path.
  • I can reopen my document and verify saved changes.
  • I can distinguish a browser from a search engine, and upload from download.
  • I can check a destination and permission request before sharing information.

Completion outcome

Demonstrate the project to a teacher or explain each step aloud. You are ready to continue when you can navigate a computer, manage basic files, and use a browser without relying on someone else to perform the steps. Then take the six-question test, which draws two easy, two medium, and two hard questions from this topic's 30-question pool. Hard questions combine these beginner skills; they do not require programming.

questions.questionText: Which part normally displays the computer's visual output?
options: Microphone
Monitor
Keyboard
Mouse
questions.explanation: The monitor displays text and images. A keyboard and mouse provide input, while a microphone receives sound.

questions.questionText: Which feature typically distinguishes a laptop from a traditional desktop with separate parts?
options: It never uses software
It cannot connect to a screen
It combines a screen, keyboard, and battery in a portable unit
It has no storage
questions.explanation: Laptops normally integrate these components and can operate on battery power. Traditional desktops commonly use separate components.

questions.questionText: Which mouse action commonly opens a menu of actions for a selected item?
options: Right-click
Move the pointer without clicking
Scroll down
Turn off the monitor
questions.explanation: A secondary or right-click commonly opens a context menu. Touchpads may provide an equivalent gesture.

questions.questionText: Which action helps you see the lower part of a long page without changing its contents?
options: Uninstall the browser
Rename the page
Delete the document
Scroll down
questions.explanation: Scrolling changes the visible portion of a page or document; it does not edit its contents.

questions.questionText: Which shortcut commonly pastes copied text in Windows and Linux editors?
options: Ctrl+S
Ctrl+V
Ctrl+A
Ctrl+C
questions.explanation: Ctrl+V commonly pastes clipboard contents. Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+A selects all, and Ctrl+C copies. macOS commonly uses Command instead.

questions.questionText: What is a folder used for?
options: Guaranteeing every file is safe
Replacing the operating system
Organizing files and other folders
Converting every file to a picture
questions.explanation: Folders organize files and subfolders. They do not automatically change formats or establish file safety.

questions.questionText: Which extension commonly identifies a plain-text file?
options: .txt
.mp3
.jpg
.pdf
questions.explanation: .txt commonly denotes plain text; .mp3 is commonly audio, .jpg an image, and .pdf a layout-preserving document format.

questions.questionText: What normally happens when you minimize a window?
options: Its application is uninstalled
All its documents are automatically deleted
The entire computer shuts down
It is hidden from the main workspace and can usually be restored
questions.explanation: Minimizing normally hides the window without quitting its app. You can restore it through the taskbar, dock, or window switcher.

questions.questionText: Which item is a web browser?
options: A folder named Downloads
Firefox
A USB charging cable
A text file named notes.txt
questions.explanation: Firefox is an application for opening web content. A folder, cable, and text document are not browsers.

questions.questionText: What does uploading a file usually mean?
options: Renaming it on your own device
Copying it from a website to your device
Sending it from your device to a remote system
Moving its window on the desktop
questions.explanation: Uploading sends data to a remote system. Downloading brings data from a remote system to your device.

questions.questionText: You copy a sentence, click at the end of your document, and paste. What should normally happen?
options: A copy appears at the insertion point while the original remains
The original sentence is removed automatically
The entire document becomes an image
The document is automatically uploaded
questions.explanation: Copy and paste duplicates selected text at the destination. It does not remove the original, convert the format, or upload the document.

questions.questionText: You want to open a file in a desktop file manager configured to use double-click. Which action is appropriate?
options: Scroll twice without selecting it
Hold the computer's power button
Rename the containing folder
Click the file twice quickly without moving the pointer much
questions.explanation: A quick double-click commonly opens a file in this configuration. Web links usually need one click; file-manager settings can vary.

questions.questionText: You minimized your editor and now want to continue the same unsaved document. What is the best next step?
options: Install another editor immediately
Restore the existing editor window from the taskbar, dock, or window switcher
Delete its shortcut
Shut down without saving
questions.explanation: Restoring the existing window returns you to that document. Minimizing does not normally close it or save its contents.

questions.questionText: Which example correctly describes a path to a project file?
options: The color of the file's icon
Only the computer's brand name
Documents/My First Computer Project/my-first-note.txt
The volume setting
questions.explanation: A path identifies folders leading to a file. Separator conventions differ by system, but the folder structure describes its location.

questions.questionText: You copy a practice file into another folder using Copy and Paste. What should you normally find?
options: The original and a separate copy in the destination
Only a renamed original in its old location
No files anywhere
The original automatically converted to PDF
questions.explanation: Copying retains the source and creates a destination copy. Moving changes location instead.

questions.questionText: A document has been edited since the last save. Which sequence best checks that the newest work was stored?
options: Minimize, then assume all changes were saved
Turn off the monitor and unplug the computer
Rename the folder without saving the document
Save, close the document, reopen the intended file, and inspect the latest text
questions.explanation: Saving and reopening the intended file verifies its persisted contents. Minimizing or changing folder names does not save unsaved edits.

questions.questionText: Where should a beginner normally look first for a file just downloaded through a browser?
options: Only in the recycle bin
The browser's download list and the selected download folder
Inside the physical keyboard
In every open calculator window
questions.explanation: The browser's download list can show the file or its location. Downloads is common, but users can choose a different folder.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes a search engine from a browser?
options: Both are physical parts inside a mouse
A browser can only display one specific search engine
A browser opens web content; a search engine is a service that finds pages using queries
A search engine is the folder holding all downloaded files
questions.explanation: A browser is an application; a search engine is a service often used within it. They perform different roles.

questions.questionText: A simple calculator app unexpectedly requests camera access. What is the safest response?
options: Deny the unexpected request and investigate why it is needed
Allow it because every app needs the camera
Disable all security protections
Share administrator credentials with the app publisher in a public form
questions.explanation: Permissions should match a legitimate task. A simple calculator ordinarily has no reason to access a camera, so unexpected access deserves scrutiny.

questions.questionText: You want to remove an application from a shared school computer. What should you do?
options: Delete a random folder inside the operating system
Remove its shortcut and assume it is uninstalled
Install an unknown cleanup tool from an advertisement
Ask the administrator and use an approved uninstall method if authorized
questions.explanation: Shared machines require permission, and apps should be removed through a supported process. Deleting a shortcut does not normally uninstall the app.

questions.questionText: You saved the project file in Downloads by mistake, but it belongs in Documents/My First Computer Project. You want one copy in the intended folder. What is the best plan?
options: Change .txt to .pdf so the computer chooses a new folder
Use a supported move operation, then verify the destination path and reopen the file
Copy it repeatedly without checking any paths
Delete Downloads before checking whether the file was saved elsewhere
questions.explanation: Moving changes the location. Checking the path and reopening the destination verifies both placement and contents without relying on assumptions.

questions.questionText: A learner renames photo.jpg to photo.pdf and expects a PDF document. What is the most accurate explanation?
options: Renaming always converts the internal data
Every image is already a valid PDF
Changing the extension alone does not convert the file; use a compatible app's export or conversion feature
The photo is permanently deleted by any rename
questions.explanation: An extension helps identify a format, but renaming does not rewrite the underlying data into another format. Real conversion requires appropriate software.

questions.questionText: Your project file is online-only in a cloud-synced folder, and tomorrow you must work without internet. What should you do now?
options: Use the provider's supported download or keep-offline option and verify it opens offline before you need it
Assume every visible filename proves its full contents are stored locally
Rename the cloud folder to Offline and do nothing else
Delete the file on the website to protect its local availability
questions.explanation: An online-only entry may not include local contents. Downloading for offline use and checking access is safer than relying on a visible filename.

questions.questionText: A website uses HTTPS and asks you to upload your project, but you do not recognize its domain. What should you conclude?
options: HTTPS guarantees the site is your teacher's site
Uploading any private document is safe if the page has a padlock
The filename alone proves the upload destination is trustworthy
HTTPS protects the connection, but you must still verify the destination and permission to share the file
questions.explanation: Encryption to a site is not proof of its trustworthiness or identity as the intended recipient. Verify the domain and share only authorized content.

questions.questionText: You saved your note, added a final sentence, and closed the editor by choosing Don't Save. After reopening the file, what should you normally expect?
options: The unsaved sentence must appear because the window closed
The last saved version, without that final unsaved sentence
No file at all because closing always deletes files
A new PDF containing the sentence
questions.explanation: In an editor without intervening autosave, discarding changes preserves the last saved version. Closing is not the same as saving.

questions.questionText: You used Save As to create a second version, edited it, and saved again. The first version still has the old text. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Save As updates every file with similar text forever
The operating system cannot store two text documents
You are editing the second version; check its filename and path to identify which file receives later saves
Renaming the monitor would synchronize the files
questions.explanation: Save As commonly changes the current document's name or location. Later saves update that current version, not every earlier copy.

questions.questionText: You have an editor and browser open. You press Select All while a browser form field has focus, expecting to select the editor document. What went wrong?
options: Shortcuts apply to the focused app or control, so you must focus the editor document first
Select All always selects every file on the computer
The keyboard can only work in one app after startup
The editor must be uninstalled before it can receive focus
questions.explanation: Keyboard input goes to the active app and focused control. Switching focus to the intended document is necessary before applying its editing shortcut.

questions.questionText: You want to try an app. A pop-up claims you must install an urgent update and enter administrator credentials before downloading it. What is the best response?
options: Follow the pop-up because urgency proves authenticity
Turn off all warnings and use the first download link
Enter a shared administrator password into the website
Dismiss the unexpected prompt, verify the app through a trusted source, and use the system's trusted update mechanism if needed
questions.explanation: Unexpected urgency and credential requests are reasons to stop and verify. Authentic installation and updates should use trusted, authorized mechanisms.

questions.questionText: You are about to submit a practice web form with an attachment. Two similarly named files exist, one with private information. What should you do before submitting?
options: Attach both files to avoid choosing
Inspect the exact file path and contents, select only the authorized practice file, review the destination and fields, then check submission confirmation
Assume the first search result is always correct
Rename the private file Practice and upload it without reading it
questions.explanation: Similar names do not establish identity or safe contents. Verify the file, its contents, the recipient, and the form before sharing, then confirm the result.

questions.questionText: You deleted a practice document from a cloud-synced folder, expecting the cloud copy to remain as a backup. What is the most accurate advice?
options: Sync can never propagate deletions
A visible cloud icon guarantees unlimited recovery
Sync may propagate deletion; check the provider's recovery tools and keep a separate backup for independent protection
Empty every recycle bin immediately to recover the file
questions.explanation: Synchronization can mirror deletions across devices and cloud storage. Recovery depends on the provider and retention policy; an independent backup offers different protection.
